Cyber security without humans? The rise of agentic AI
The next evolution of cyber security may be autonomous, but industry leaders warn that trust, governance and human judgement can't be automated
Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) may be enabling unprecedented levels of automation in cyber security. Still, enterprise leaders in the United Arab Emirates (UAE) believe organisations are not yet ready to remove humans from decision-making.
“Automation is not something new; we’ve been doing automation for decades,” said Mohammad Al Rais, senior director of group IT at ENOC. “When we talk about agentic AI, it’s automation with a brain.”
Speaking during a panel discussion on the future of autonomous AI in cyber security, Al Rais argued that agentic AI should be viewed as the next evolution of automation rather than a replacement for human expertise. “It’s a near-human kind of process, yet that needs guidance,” he said. “Humans and agentic AI might be similar – both can go wrong, and both can go beyond the ethical part. What guides them is the rules that we set.”
Organisations are increasingly exploring how agentic AI can improve security operations by automating tasks such as threat analysis, alert triage and incident investigation. At ENOC, Al Rais said the company has already begun extending AI capabilities into its cyber security function.
“We have extended our AI capability to the cyber team,” he said. “They are using it for alert triage. They are using it for analysing logs and threats.”
Asked whether he trusts AI systems to perform these activities, Al Rais said confidence is still being built: “We are in the process of trusting.”
For Abdalla Ahmed Mohammed Al Ali, senior director of IT at DMCC, the decision to introduce agentic AI depends largely on the risk level associated with a particular process. “When it comes to AI adoption, it is a revolutionary technology, and we can see the value and the impact.”
Al Ali said AI can deliver significant benefits when applied to repetitive tasks that do not involve highly sensitive or business-critical outcomes.
“As long as that service is not risky, is not too critical and is repetitive, then we try to use AI to make things easier and seamless,” he said. “Ultimately, we want to make sure that the outcome of leveraging that is beneficial for the team as well as for the members and stakeholders.”
However, he cautioned that the equation changes when AI is introduced into systems that could affect an organisation’s reputation, finances or critical operations. “If you have critical services which might have an impact on the reputation of the organisation, or a financial impact, then we have to be extremely conscious,” he added.
While Al Ali said he supports introducing AI across a broad range of use cases, he stressed that organisations must carefully assess where human oversight remains necessary: “It depends on the ROI [return on investment], the impact, the criticality and the severity. Based on these factors, I will decide whether the human needs to be in the loop or whether it can operate without the human.”
Noman Rasheed, CIO at Dubai Islamic Bank, shared the same point of view and argued that governance and control mechanisms become even more important as AI systems gain greater autonomy: “The human role is extremely important. There is no concept of handing over processes to AI without control and validity. This is where humans play a role.”
Rasheed noted that concerns about AI making mistakes should be viewed in the same way organisations have traditionally approached the risk of human error: “The concern has always been whether humans can make mistakes. The answer is yes, but does that mean you take humans out of the loop? The answer is no – what you do is deploy controls.”
According to Rasheed, the same principle applies to agentic AI systems: “We need guardrails to protect and observe what the agents and AI are doing. There is no question about humans going out of the loop. Humans will always play a role in different capacities throughout the journey.”
Rasheed also argued that organisations should apply zero-trust principles to AI in the same way they do to users and devices: “We have one fundamental rule: zero trust. There is no way we trust humans. There is no way we trust machines. There is no way we trust AI.”
The growing adoption of agentic AI also introduces new risks around model integrity, data quality and AI security, particularly in highly regulated sectors such as banking. “There will always be a place for humans in the AI and agentic AI era; humans are responsible for making sure that agentic AI is not being tampered with, poisoned or altered,” said Rasheed.
“Imagine showing the CFO wrong numbers because the model was poisoned and there was no human to verify the data,” he added. “Any entity could collapse. The decisions being taken based on pure AI would be completely wrong.”
As organisations continue to experiment with agentic AI across cyber security operations, the panellists agreed that the technology’s success will depend not only on its capabilities, but also on the governance frameworks surrounding it.

items.body:
The Barcode Warehouse teams with Lincolnshire Co-op on self-checkouts roll-out across food stores
The Barcode Warehouse is working with Lincolnshire Co-op on the roll-out of a new self-checkout solution. Lincolnshire Co-op, which operates more than 220 outlets across Lincolnshire and neighbouring counties, including food stores, pharmacies, post offices and travel branches, is expanding self-service checkout options across its food store estate as part of its investment in enhancing customer experience.
Andy Warman, Chief Commercial and Transformation Officer at Lincolnshire Co-op, says: “The introduction of self-checkouts across our food stores represents an important step in enhancing the shopping experience for our customers. Working with The Barcode Warehouse, we have delivered a solution that provides greater convenience, reduces queuing times, and gives customers more choice in how they shop. This investment reflects our ongoing commitment to continuing to deliver high standards of customer service and embracing innovation technology that adds value for our communities.”
The Barcode Warehouse has supplied and supported the retailer's in-store technology estate for more than three years. Today, it supplies Point of Sale equipment, handheld devices for stock management and pricing updates, reduced to clear printing solutions and managed services support across the business.
Jason Datt, Head of Retail at The Barcode Warehouse, says: "Retailers are increasingly looking at how technology can remove friction from the shopping journey while helping stores operate more efficiently. Self-checkout has become an important part of that balance, giving customers greater choice and convenience while helping colleagues focus on delivering excellent service where it's needed most."
“Our role goes beyond supplying technology. We work closely with retailers to understand their operational challenges, customer expectations and long-term goals, helping them identify solutions that deliver measurable benefits in-store. Through our long-standing relationship with Lincolnshire Co-op, we've been able to support the roll-out of a self-checkout solution that not only enhances the customer experience but also provides the flexibility and scalability needed to support future store innovation."
Sam Eade, Project Manager at Lincolnshire Co-op, says: “From the initial planning stages to implementation and colleague training, this project with The Barcode Warehouse has been a true team effort. We’re proud of what has been achieved through this fantastic collaboration and it’s rewarding to already see the benefits of faster transactions for customers and more time for colleagues to be available on the shopfloor.”
The deployment also marks the first UK retail implementation delivered under the partnership between The Barcode Warehouse and CCL, a provider of self-checkout and retail hardware solutions, announced last year. The project will see around 155 CCL Z2 21.5" Windows self-checkout units installed across 74 Lincolnshire Co-op food stores, with a further 21 stores set for deployment in late 2026.

Our 2025 hall of fame entrants were revealed during a sold out event which took place at The HAC on 16th October and consisted of a drinks reception, three course meal, and awards ceremony presided over by award winning comedian, actress and writer Tiff Stevenson.
In his welcome speech, Scott Thompson, Founder and Editor, RTIH, said: “This is the awards’ fifth year as a physical event. We started off with just 30 people at the South Place Hotel not far from here, then moved to London Bridge Hotel, then The Barbican, and last year RIBA’s HQ in the West End.”
“But I’m conscious of the fact that, to quote the legend that is Taylor Swift, You’re only as hot as your last hit, baby. So, this year we’ve moved to our biggest venue yet, and also pulled in our largest number of entries to date and broken attendance records.”

items.body:
Industry first as Hozelock opts to deploy Polytag technology across its garden products range
Polytag has partnered with Hozelock, a manufacturer of garden watering and outdoor products, to introduce smart QR codes across its garden product range. The deployment brings connected product experiences to the garden and outdoor sector for the first time.
By scanning the codes, Hozelock customers can access product specific guidance, including how to guides and videos, while the company gains new insight into how and where its products are being used.
The smart QR codes, powered by Polytag's platform, have been added to Hozelock products available through retailers including B&Q. When scanned, the codes can direct consumers to content tailored to their market and device language, enabling Hozelock to provide relevant information across its international markets using a single QR code.
This is particularly valuable for Hozelock's range of technical and higher value garden products, where packaging alone cannot always display the level of information customers may need. The digital connection also provides a foundation for future product level information requirements, including Digital Product Passports, allowing Hozelock to build on the infrastructure already in place as these requirements are rolled out.
The deployment also gives Hozelock visibility beyond the point of purchase. Through the Polytag platform, the company can see where and when customers are engaging with its products, providing data that was previously unavailable once a product had left the retailer. Data collected between November 2025 and August 2026 has revealed high levels of engagement, generating 11,399 QR scans and over 3,610 minutes of engagement time, with an average dwell time of 19 seconds, exceeding the reported industry average of 7.4 seconds. Engagement has been recorded across 63 product SKUs and 1,344 locations, providing further insight into how and where consumers are interacting with Hozelock products.
The technology has also been used by Hozelock as a marketing engagement tool. Ahead of major industry exhibitions, including Spoga+Gafa and Glee, QR codes were included on event invitations, enabling recipients to access teaser content showcasing upcoming product launches before their official unveiling at the shows.
Alice Rackley, CEO at Polytag, comments: “Hozelock is a great example of how smart QR technology can create value for both brands and consumers. Customers can access useful, product specific information at the moment they need it, while Hozelock gains visibility into how people are engaging with its products after purchase. For a brand selling technical products across multiple markets, the ability to deliver relevant information in the right language through a single QR code is incredibly powerful. The engagement we're seeing also shows the appetite consumers have for useful digital content that helps them get more from the products they buy.”
Alina Gordon, Marketing and Communications Executive at Hozelock, says: “Our goal is always to make the customer experience as simple and helpful as possible. By incorporating Polytag QR codes onto our packaging, we're giving consumers instant access to the information they need while creating a more connected relationship between our products and our customers. The technology has also provided exciting opportunities to engage audiences in new ways, such as supporting product launch campaigns and exhibition activity.”

These companies operate across the omnichannel retail landscape (stores, online, mobile, supply chain, payments etc).
Our judging panel, including Vineta Bajaj, Group CFO, Holland & Barrett, Dan McGrath, JD Group Customer Operations, JD Sports, Dr. Astha Purohit, Director of Product Management, Customer Data and Identity, Walmart, and Paula Bobbett, Chief Data and Digital Officer, Boots, provided feedback on those who have the most innovative, forward thinking technology offerings and are also best addressing retailers' current challenges, painpoints, and opportunities.

1. Retailer problem fit - how meaningful, strategic, and widely felt the retailer pain being addressed is.
2. Production traction in retail (2025–2026) - real named retailer deployments, pilots. 
3. Innovation and defensibility - genuine technical novelty paired with a defensible competitive position.

items.body:
Now you can get your High Street bank to pay you 8% on your cash savings: SYLVIA MORRIS
By SYLVIA MORRIS, THIS IS MONEY AND DAILY MAIL SAVINGS EXPERT
Updated:
Savings rates are up across the board this month (hurrah!) so it’s a good time to make sure you’re not missing out.
Leave your savings where they are and you could be walking away from hundreds of pounds in potential interest.
You can now get up to 8 per cent with a certain type of account. This even beats the average growth of the UK stock market and, unlike investing, there is no risk of losing your money.
High Street banks offer so-called regular saver accounts to attract current account customers.
These accounts let you save a set amount each month, typically for a year, and often pay far more than ordinary savings accounts. Start by checking what your current account provider offers.
While many banks pay paltry rates on easy-access savings, their regular saver accounts often pay between 5 per cent and 8 per cent on monthly deposits of up to £250 or £300.
Savings rates are up across the board this month, so act now to make sure you're not missing out on hundreds of pounds of potential interest
Ideally, set up a standing order just after payday and save little and often. At the end of the year, move the money elsewhere, as many banks transfer balances into low-paying, easy-access accounts.
Even though interest is taxable, many savers will earn more from a regular saver than from a tax-free cash Isa paying around 4 per cent.
Basic-rate taxpayers can earn up to £1,000 in savings interest before paying tax, higher-rate taxpayers £500, while additional-rate taxpayers have no allowance.
For example, saving £100 a month at Santander’s market-leading 8 per cent rate would leave you with £1,252 after a year, including £52 interest.
The same amount saved in a cash Isa paying 4 per cent would grow to £1,226, including £26 interest. Some providers allow withdrawals while others penalise savers who dip into their cash.
Santander pays 8 per cent on savings of up to £200 a month and allows access to the money.
First Direct pays 7 per cent on up to £300 a month but requires the account to be closed if money is withdrawn, reducing the rate paid to 1.05 per cent. Co-op Bank also pays 7 per cent and allows withdrawals.
Lloyds, Halifax and Bank of Scotland pay 6.25 per cent on up to £250 a month. NatWest offers 5.25 per cent, while HSBC and TSB pay 5 per cent.
Nationwide and Virgin Money both pay 6.5 per cent. Nationwide limits customers to four withdrawals a year, with the rate falling to 1.05 per cent after that.
Chase has launched a 6.5 per cent regular saver allowing deposits of up to £300 a month.
For those unwilling to open a linked current account, Monmouthshire Building Society offers 6 per cent on contributions of up to £500 a month.
All the accounts mentioned are protected by the Financial Services Compensation Scheme.

If you want to make the most of your savings, checking the top rates and moving to a better deal is essential, as is using a cash Isa to beat savings tax.

items.title: Wayfair ups investment in sports for values-focused brand platform
items.summary: The retailer is amplifying its latest effort by increasing advertising investment across the networks airing football games to five times its previous spend.
items.body:
Dive Brief:
- Wayfair has teamed with Los Angeles Rams quarterback Matthew Stafford for a new brand platform called “Wayfair Delivers,” according to a press release.
- Key to the effort is a 30-second spot starring Stafford alongside his wife and four kids as they use Wayfair to furnish their family space. The ad, made in-house with support from Paramount Media Labs, debuted during “Monday Night Football” on ABC and ESPN.
- Wayfair is also upping its focus on sports through an increase in advertising investment across the networks airing football games to five times its previous spend. The move follows a rise in orders placed during Q2, driven primarily by mobile shoppers.
Dive Insight:
The “Wayfair Delivers” platform kicks off a new long-term brand strategy focused on the qualities, like value and trusted service, that the home furnishings retailer offers consumers, per details shared with sister publication Marketing Dive. The move also sees the retailer upping its bet on live sports, which remain an attractive advertising opportunity for brands despite the rise in streaming TV. Sports provide advertisers access to a broad audience, with nearly half of the U.S. population identifying as live sports viewers, according to Emarketer.
“Wayfair Delivers” kicks off with an ad starring Stafford, who was named the 2025 Associated Press NFL MVP, alongside his wife, Kelly, and their four daughters. The spot starts by touting Stafford’s football credentials before abruptly transitioning to his chaotic life at home, complete with pillows soaring through the air, toys on display and furniture that has seen better days. The Staffords then place a Wayfair order for furniture that proves more functional for the family.
Along with the ad, Wayfair is calling attention to value-focused offerings, including Wayfair Verified — its collection of items hand-vetted for quality — and the Wayfair Rewards loyalty program. “Wayfair Delivers” will span linear TV, connected TV and social channels, with the Stafford ad to air on ABC, ESPN, CBS and NBC.
In addition to its hefty increase in ad investment, Wayfair is deepening its investment in football by sponsoring and decorating the set for CBS Sports’ Sunday morning football pregame show. The retailer will also sponsor B/R NFL Draft Live in April 2027 through a partnership with Bleacher Report.
Though the broader furniture category is stuck in a sales slump, Wayfair has recently seen bright spots. The company’s Q2 revenue increased 7.5% versus the year-ago period, growth that was driven by momentum in orders, which were up 6% year over year for a total of 10.6 million. Of total orders, Wayfair customers placed 64.1% via mobile device, an increase from 62.9% the previous year.
Wayfair has worked to enhance its online shopping experience, including through a partnership with Google earlier this year around artificial intelligence-powered discovery. The company has also focused on growing its brick-and-mortar footprint.

items.title: JD Sports to open more than 140 shops in Mexico as it steps up overseas expansion
items.summary: A partnership with Grupo Axo, which helps brands grow in Mexico, Chile, Peru and Uruguay, will launch the JD brand in the region.
items.body:
JD Sports to open more than 140 shops in Mexico as it steps up overseas expansion
JD Sports Fashion has unveiled plans to open more than 140 shops in Mexico as it steps up its expansion overseas.
The Lancashire-based retail chain said it wanted to tap into the fast-growing activewear market.
The partnership with Grupo Axo, which helps brands grow in Mexico, Chile, Peru and Uruguay, will launch the JD brand in the region.
Starting in 2027, Axo will operate more than 140 JD stores in Mexico, with key shops expected to eventually be expanded and refurbished under the group’s ‘bigger and better’ format, according to the retailer.
JD said Mexico’s activewear market is being driven by interests like running, football and fashion, helped by a large population of shoppers under the age of 25.
Boss Regis Schultz said: ‘Bringing JD to this thriving market is an exciting milestone in our story. JD’s product offering aligns closely with consumer demand in Mexico.’
JD Sports Fashion has formed a partnership with Grupo Axo and unveiled plans to open more than 140 shops in Mexico

items.title: Sephora furthers UK ambitions via M&S shop-in-shops
items.summary: The tie-up resembles the beauty retailer’s partnership with Kohl’s in the U.S., which was a sales and traffic driver until this year.
items.body:
Dive Brief:
- 
Sephora has partnered with Marks & Spencer to bring “Sephora at M&S” shops into 100 of the U.K. retailer’s stores and to its website, starting next spring.
- 
M&S said the spaces will boost traffic from new and existing customers. The retailer’s share of the U.K. beauty market in the 12 months ending mid-July is a little over 1%.
- 
For Sephora, the shops will extend its reach in the U.K., according to a joint press release.
Dive Insight:
The beauty market in the U.K. is approaching roughly $7 billion and grew 1.2% in the 12 months ending July 19, according to WorldPanel by Numerator data cited in the press release from M&S and Sephora Tuesday.
These retailers have come together in their efforts to grow their share. For M&S, the Sephora spaces will enhance a wider push there that includes investments into a private-label beauty assortment, according to a statement from John Lyttle, managing director of fashion, home and beauty at M&S. The partnership is part of an ongoing transformation of the beauty offer, he said.
“Beauty is an important category for M&S, with the potential to attract new customers to shop with us and give existing customers the opportunity to shop with us more often,” he said.
This was the hope at Kohl’s in the U.S. when that retailer forged a similar alliance with Sephora in 2020. The U.S. department store touted the shop-in-shops as a traffic and sales driver for years. But so far this year they have been a drag on Kohl’s results.
But the similarities don’t go all that deep because M&S is starting off the relationship with more advantages of its own, including some traction with younger consumers, according to GlobalData Managing Director Neil Saunders.
“M&S is in a strong position, and it already has plenty of traffic drivers to stores — especially the food offer. M&S also has its own beauty and personal care assortment, albeit one that is fairly narrow,” he said by email. “Comparatively, Kohl’s added Sephora to a core proposition that was struggling and the offer jarred a little with the rest of the Kohl’s store. The move by M&S is tactical. It was already building up its credibility with younger shoppers and it sees Sephora as a targeted way to get more of those cohorts in its stores.”
The tie-up with M&S furthers Sephora’s ambitions in the U.K., too, by combining its prestige beauty expertise with the retailer’s brick-and-mortar infrastructure, according to Catherine Spindler, Sephora’s president of Europe and Middle East.
“Our UK launch has been such a huge success, that we wanted to go further and faster,” Spindler said in a statement. “Our partnership with M&S is the next evolution of this strategy, introducing a retail model that complements our existing formats and allows us to build on the strength of the Sephora brand in the UK.”

items.title: Post Office boss calls for tax breaks to save rural branches
items.summary: The boss of the Post Office has urged ministers to save village branches from crippling hikes in business rates.
items.body:
Post Office boss calls for tax breaks to save rural branches
The boss of the Post Office has urged ministers to save village branches from crippling hikes in business rates.
Chief executive Neil Brocklehurst said post offices play a ‘similarly vital role in communities’ to pubs, which have been handed support with the commercial property levy.
He said post offices also need ‘urgent help’ in the form of ‘targeted relief’.
Controversial changes in last year’s Budget mean post offices will pay nearly £45million in business rates this year – an increase of £29million.
Nearly 600 branches will have to pay rates for the first time.
Writing for the Daily Mail, Brocklehurst said: ‘There is a contradiction at the heart of the Government’s ambition for growth. We say we want thriving high streets and essential services within easy reach of every community. But many of the businesses delivering exactly that are facing a sharp increase in costs.’
Post offices will pay almost £45million in business rates this year - an increase of £29million
He added: ‘Government has already accepted that pubs merit financial support because of their wider social and economic contribution to communities – with a 20 per cent cut to their business rates bill set to come into effect in England next year. Few would dispute the important role pubs play in bringing people together. But post offices play a similarly vital role in communities.
‘If Government is serious about growth in every postcode, then it should recognise the unique role post offices play in making that growth possible. That is why postmasters are calling for targeted business rates relief.’
There were 11,708 post office branches in the UK as of February 2026, according to a recent report from the Office for National Statistics. It said that the number of branches has remained relatively stable since 2009.
The business is hoping to extend its network and opening hours by 2030.
Brocklehurst is just the latest businessman to call for reform of the rates system.
Writing for the Daily Mail on Monday, Mark Allan, the boss of commercial property giant Landsec, said a shake-up was required to help firms tackle Britain’s youth unemployment crisis.
He said the growing number of youngsters not in education, employment or training – so-called NEETs – was ‘a catastrophe in slow motion for our economy’.
‘It’s become increasingly clear that addressing the NEET crisis can’t be viewed solely through the narrow lens of skills and education,’ said Allan.
‘It should go without saying that businesses also need the capacity to create entry-level jobs, something that has been made harder by the decisions taken by successive governments.’
Post offices play a vital role in our communities
By Neil Brocklehurst, chief executive of the Post Office
During his first few weeks in office, Prime Minister Andy Burnham has made good growth in every postcode a defining objective of his Government. It’s a simple proposition. Economic success should not be confined to city centres or a handful of prosperous regions. It should be felt in our daily lives: on high streets and in villages across the UK.
Post Office chief executive Neil Brocklehurst
If we are serious about good growth in every postcode, we must be equally serious about what will make that possible.
Visit a post office on any morning and you’ll see what that looks like in practice. A small business owner depositing the previous day’s cash takings. Vinted and TikTok shop traders dropping off parcels. People of all ages depositing and withdrawing cash and paying their bills. These are ordinary moments, but together they are the building blocks of local economic activity and community life.
With 11,500 branches across the UK, a thriving Post Office network is not merely an accessory to growth in every postcode. It is a driving factor that makes growth possible.
Every week, more than ten million people and businesses visit a post office. The value of these visits goes further than just the money spent in branch: someone who drops off a parcel or pays a bill at the post office is likely to visit nearby businesses too. Collectively, this creates a halo effect worth £3billion of spend in nearby shops annually.
And then there’s the social impact of having a post office nearby. The public tells us there is a connection between community identity, pride and the state of the local high street. Over half say that a local post office fosters a sense of belonging to the community and is important to its identity.
Yet there is a contradiction at the heart of the Government’s ambition for growth. We say we want thriving high streets and essential services within easy reach of every community. But many of the businesses delivering exactly that are facing a sharp increase in costs.
Most post offices are independently run small businesses and they earn remuneration for each transaction carried out in branch. Now faced with rising costs, postmasters continue to tell me they are struggling. We are making urgent and essential changes to how Post Office operates to address this. Last year, we increased postmaster remuneration by over £86million – but it’s not enough against a backdrop of rising costs. For some, particularly in rural and isolated communities, these additional costs come at a time when margins are already under significant pressure.
Government has already accepted that pubs merit financial support because of their wider social and economic contribution to communities – with a 20 per cent cut to their business rates bill set to come into effect in England next year. Few would dispute the important role pubs play in bringing people together. But post offices play a similarly vital role in communities.
Recent changes to the business rates system mean post offices across the UK are forecast to pay almost £45million in business rates this year. That's around £29million more than branches paid under the previous relief system. Nearly 600 additional post offices will begin paying business rates for the first time, while the average bill is expected to rise to around £3,700. For rural post offices, the increase is particularly stark, with average rates bills expected to be around four times higher in 2026 than they were in 2023.
This burden is not just felt by the postmaster. If a branch closes, it is felt by the small business owner who relies on Post Office for banking services, or the vulnerable customer who prefers that face-to-face support, as well as nearby shops who see their footfall affected.
If the Government is serious about growth in every postcode, then it should recognise the unique role post offices play in making that growth possible.
That is why postmasters are calling for targeted business rates relief. This is not a request for special treatment. It is recognition that post offices are different from other retailers. They are community infrastructure: supporting other local businesses and providing services that many people would otherwise struggle to access.
The conversation about growth can often feel distant from people's daily lives. But growth in every postcode is not an abstract slogan. It is a small business able to keep trading, a busy high street, a village retaining vital services. Across Britain, postmasters are supporting good growth in every postcode every day, but they need urgent help in order to continue doing so.

items.title: Boss of B&Q owner Kingfisher sounds alarm over business rates raid on larger stores
items.summary: The boss of B&Q owner Kingfisher has sounded the alarm over the risk of a business rates raid on larger stores in next month's Budget.
items.body:
Boss of B&Q owner Kingfisher sounds alarm over business rates raid on larger stores
The boss of B&Q owner Kingfisher has sounded the alarm over the risk of a business rates raid on larger stores in next month’s Budget.
Thierry Garnier joined a chorus of retail chiefs in urging Labour not to hit big premises as part of reforms to the hated commercial property tax.
Garnier said: ‘Big stores are very often big anchors in retail parks and in high streets, large employers in cities. So we very much hope that the larger stores won’t be penalised in the coming weeks.’
The comments came as Kingfisher – which also owns Screwfix as well as European brands Castorama and Brico Depot – upgraded its full-year profit outlook after publishing strong first half results.
That was despite a setback for B&Q, which saw summer sales hit by the heatwave and weak demand for its bathroom range, which is now being revamped. Instead, customers preferred to splash out on their kitchens.
Garnier said: ‘People are spending more money on their kitchen today than on their bathroom… a more important part of our lives, it’s becoming a more important room in the house, and we see that across Europe – a more positive trend on kitchen than bathroom.’
B&Q has more than 300 stores
Shares rose 9pc in early trading as the UK-listed group said adjusted profits for the six months to 31 July rose 10pc to £404m, driven by higher margins and cost control.
It is now forecasting full-year profits of £595m-£635m, versus previous guidance of £565m-£625m.
However, like-for-like sales rose by just 0.3pc and Garnier admitted that ‘the consumer environment remains mixed’.
In the UK, Screwfix sales jumped 5.6pc in the first half but B&Q struggled, with a fall of 2.9pc. The brand saw a notable 8.1pc slump in demand for ‘big ticket’ items in the second quarter.
Screwfix has more than 981 stores in the UK and Ireland while B&Q has 318.
Garnier, who is quitting Kingfisher to become the boss of Netherlands-based supermarket group Ahold Delhaize shrugged off a question about his departure.
He said: ‘I’m fully committed and focused on Kingfisher. The board has a well-prepared succession plan. The search is ongoing and moving at pace.’
On the Budget, Garnier said: ‘We believe that retail is a powerful engine for growth, it is an engine of employment, and we hope the government can see it in the same way.
‘Stability and certainty is always what you look for as a business.
‘For us, the number one priority is business rates… in the longer term, we need a level playing field between bricks-and-mortar and online players.
‘When you are a brick and mortar retailer and when you are a pure online company you don’t pay the same tax and that will create more and more issues in the future.’
But his fears over the impact of business rate hikes on larger stores echo those expressed by the bosses of other major retailers in recent weeks.
Sports Direct billionaire Mike Ashley has said the Government would be ‘simply delusional’ to heap more pressure on big retailers.
Some firms fear Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Chancellor John Healey are plotting a fresh business rates raid on large shops to fund lower bills for pubs and music venues.
They are particularly concerned that rates paid by large stores, which are deemed to have a rateable value of £500,000 or more, will be increased.
Outgoing John Lewis boss Peter Ruis said earlier this month that it would have ‘a terrible impact for all retailers’.

items.title: Debenhams returns to profit: Is the embattled department store finally turning a corner?
items.summary: We look at what caused the downfall of this titan of the high street, and whether its transformation efforts are paying off.
items.body:
Debenhams returns to profit: Is the embattled department store finally turning a corner?
Once a retail titan, Debenhams has had a difficult few years.
Fast-fashion firm Boohoo bought the department store chain out of administration in 2021, dispensing with its shops and going online-only in a major blow to the high street.
Debenhams has also been the subject of a long-running spat with retail veteran Mike Ashley, whose Frasers Group is its biggest shareholder.
More recently, Debenhams sold off youth brand Nasty Gal and announced the sudden departure of its chairman.
But it is not all bad. The retailer has long trailed a turnaround in its fortunes, and last week revealed its earnings had bounced back into profit in the previous six-month period.
Debenhams, which also owns the Karen Millen and Pretty Little Thing brands, cheered stronger sales and anticipates earnings to improve as it cuts costs.
Boss Dan Finley said: 'Our turnaround continues at pace. This is a strong first half, and, importantly, one where growth accelerated as we went through it.'
What caused Debenhams' downfall, and will its transformation efforts pay off?
Collapse: Debenhams went into administration in April 2020 and Boohoo Group, now known as Debenhams Group, purchased its brand and website
From high street giant to online challenger
Debenhams was once one of the best-known department store chains, but struggled with lower profits, rising debts and shoppers switching to online.
Its collapse in April 2020 led to the closure of all 124 of its shops and 12,000 job losses. Two hundred years of retail history disappeared in the blink of an eye.
Boohoo Group, founded in 2006 by Mahmud Kamani and Carol Kane, bought the Debenhams brand and website for £55million in 2021.
Following the acquisition, Boohoo Group rebranded itself in March 2025 to become Debenhams Group, operating across five core brands: Debenhams, Karen Millen, boohoo, BoohooMAN, Pretty Little Thing as well as several other labels such as Oasis and Warehouse.
Dan Finley: The current boss took up the role in 2024 and quickly launched a turnaround plan
Suddenly, Debenhams Group had to take the old-style Debenhams people knew and loved and turn it into a modern online retail brand without any physical shops.
Dan Finley joined Debenhams Group as chief executive of Debenhams in January 2022. He became the boss of the wider group two years later.
In a BBC podcast this year, Finley admitted he was unsure about taking on such a challenging role.
What went wrong for Debenhams?
The years that have followed the Boohoo group's acquisition of the Debenhams brand and website have been torrid.
Debenhams Group and other online retailers enjoyed a surge in demand during the pandemic, when many households went online to buy comfortable clothing to work and rest at home while high streets were closed.
But once shops reopened, retailers saw fresh competition from cheap Chinese sellers like Shein and Temu, as well as secondhand marketplaces such as Vinted and Depop. Online firms like Debenhams Group, and particularly its 'youth' brands, took a hit.
On a single day in July 2020, more than £1billion was wiped off the value of Debenhams Group, then still known as Boohoo Group, after it was revealed workers were paid less than the minimum wage at its Leicester garment factory.
In November 2024, Debenhams Group launched an investor cash call and raised just shy of £40million. Losses across Debenhams Group were widening and a spat with Frasers Group's boss, billionaire Mike Ashley ramped up.
In 2024, interim results showed Debenhams Group's losses had more than quadrupled. The group cut more than 1,000 jobs in the year to the end of February 2024 as its net debt rose to £95million.
It was also urging investors to reject Ashley's attempt to install himself as chief executive of Debenhams Group at an emergency meeting.
Billionaire Ashley, a shareholder in Debenhams Group, had wanted to acquire Debenhams physical shops but missed out on a deal.
By March 2025, Finley said sales for the group's founding brand, Boohoo, as well as BoohooMAN and Pretty Little Thing, had fallen sharply as 'we lost our way'.
Later that year, pre-tax losses widened to £263.9million, from £164.4million a year earlier, as revenue fell 12 per cent.
A tarnished reputation, dwindling sales, more competition and a growing debt pile left the group in need of a radical transformation.
Change is under way
That has seen Debenhams Group pivot to a marketplace-led business model that it says is 'capital-lite, stock-lite, cost-lite and cash generative'.
A marketplace model is when a retailer's website acts as a shop window, allowing third-party brands to sell items on its platform for a fee instead of stocking them itself.
Debenhams wants marketplace activity to account for well over half of gross merchandise value (GMV). This is the total value of goods sold before fees and returns.
When Finley became the group chief executive in November 2024, he began a multi-year transformation plan but warned it would take time, prompting nervousness among investors.
Debenhams Group has automated parts of its supply chain, and cut investment in brands like Warehouse, Oasis, Wallis and Dorothy Perkins.
This month, it sold its Sheffield distribution centre for £90million, with the lease reassigned to Primark. It also sold youth brand Nasty Gal to New York-based White Space, which also owns Von Dutch, for nearly £12million.
Row: Debenhams Group has been embroiled in various spats with shareholder Mike Ashley
Jonathan De Mello, founder of retail consultants JDM Retail, told This is Money: 'The group initially floundered because it was weighed down by an asset-heavy infrastructure, soaring logistics costs, and massive customer return rates just as the post-pandemic online shopping boom collapsed.
'Unwinding a legacy fast-fashion empire is taking a long time because transitioning millions of customers and thousands of suppliers onto an entirely new tech and operational ecosystem requires a total structural overhaul.'
Has the group reached a turning point?
The sale of the group's Sheffield distribution centre is significant and should leave Debenhams Group's net debt at a negligible level by February 2027.
Debt has been a key sticking point for investors, so the offloading of lease costs will go some way in strengthening its bottom line.
In June 2026, the group said annual losses before tax fell to £108.6million in the year ending February 28, an improvement on the previous year.
In its most recent update, Debenhams Group said it expected earnings to continue to improve amid further cost cuts.
Adjusted earnings jumped 13.9 per cent to £24million, driven by the Debenhams brand, which accounted for 41 per cent of GMV.
The firm said it was on track to secure £100million in cost savings by next year.
On September 18, Debenhams Group announced its chairman, Tim Morris, was leaving the business with immediate effect, replaced by Iain McDonald.
McDonald, who is a significant shareholder in Debenhams Group, was previously on the firm's board from June 2017 to February 2026.
Debenhams Group said the reappointment came as its 'focus moves to rebuilding equity value' in the business after making progress in its turnaround efforts.
Mike Ashley's Frasers Group previously wrote to Morris threatening to hold a shareholder vote over his position at the business.
Jonathan De Mello added: 'While the results show the turnaround strategy entails a necessary pivot toward a lower-risk, asset-light digital marketplace model - evidenced by the offloading of the Sheffield automation hub and the Nasty Gal brand - it is premature to say the group has turned a corner.
'Fragile consumer confidence and intense competition from aggressive, ultra-cheap global players like Shein and Temu continue to heavily impact the business, meaning that while Q2 volume ticked up slightly to 2.9 per cent, Debenhams Group is still very much in financial triage mode as it attempts to permanently stabilise its baseline.'
Are Debenhams shares a buy?
Last autumn, shares in Aim-listed Debenhams Group plummeted to as low as 11.3p, but they have since recovered to around 25p.
The latest trading update offers some relief to investors, as Debenhams Group continues to cut its debt and boost earnings.
Russ Mould, investment director at AJ Bell, added: 'Several key brands returned to growth and the core Debenhams brand is also performing robustly despite a backdrop which is about as gloomy as a wet day in late November.'
He added: 'Critically the company has made real progress with its balance sheet, partly thanks to disposals and as it focuses more heavily on cash generation. This will inspire greater confidence in the group's ability to see its way through what looks set to be a testing period.'
Others think the retail group could still run into issues.
Lale Akoner, an analyst at eToro, said: 'We still think that the shares remain a high-risk turnaround bet. Investors accepting volatility may see value, but sustained sales growth and positive free cash flow would provide proof.'

items.title: Gen Z gives High Street a boost by flocking to TikTok-famous stores
items.summary: Gen Z customers are giving the High Street a welcome lift by travelling up to an hour and a half to visit small independent shops made famous online.
items.body:
Gen Z gives High Street a boost by flocking to TikTok-famous stores
Gen Z customers are giving the High Street a welcome lift by travelling up to an hour-and-a-half to visit independent shops made famous online.
The findings suggest stores suffering from the switch to e-commerce could gain a new lease of life through social media.
Research showed 80 per cent of Gen Z consumers, those born between 1997 and 2012, had visited an independent shop after finding it on sites such as Instagram and TikTok, credit card giant American Express revealed – even if it took 95 minutes to get there.
Businesses benefiting include Randalls sweet seller in Market Harborough, Leicestershire, and Humble Crumble, a pudding shop in London’s Borough Market.
Dan Edelman, at Amex, said: ‘Social media discovery is translating directly into visits and spending with small, independent firms.
With its growing influence and spending power, Gen Z is showcasing new opportunities for businesses to boost revenue, build loyalty and bring more people to Britain’s high streets.’
TikTok impact: Gen Z customers are giving the High Street a welcome lift
The findings on the ‘viral pilgrimage’ economy shed light on the behaviour of youngsters who can sometimes be seen congregating at certain shops, cafes or restaurants.
They showed 62 per cent of Gen Z consumers actively look up businesses on social media before visiting and 58 per cent say it led them to a firm they would not otherwise have found.
Most visit within a week of first seeing it online and one in five plan a day out around such a trip.
Consultancy Retail Economics found independent businesses captured half of ‘social-influenced High Street spending’ by Gen Z.

items.title: Demand for hair treatment soars to combat side effects of fat jabs
items.summary: Growing demand for weight-loss drugs has boosted sales of hair products, according to Superdrug and Boots.
items.body:
Demand for hair treatment soars to combat side effects of fat jabs
Growing demand for weight-loss drugs has boosted sales of hair products, according to Superdrug and Boots.
The drugs - sold under brand names Mounjaro and Wegovy in the UK - are taken as a weekly injection and trick the body into thinking it is full.
But users can suffer from hair thinning or hair loss and are now seeking help.
Online doctor appointments for hair loss have grown 14.9 per cent over the past year while sales of medicated hair care are up 28.8 per cent over two years, according to Superdrug.
The chemist also said that hair treatments have risen 27.7 per cent since 2024, coinciding with an increase in fat jab usage.
Around 6 per cent of households now have at least one user of the appetite-suppressing drugs, compared to 2.3 per cent in 2024, according to researchers at Worldpanel by Numerator. Some 1.9million Britons are thought to be using the jabs.
Shoppers are increasingly looking for products that claim to keep their hair healthy - including tackling side effects of weight-loss drugs.
Chelsey Saunders, director of haircare, skincare and fragrance at Boots, said: ‘As conversations around GLP-1 medications continue to grow, we’re also seeing an increased interest in hair and scalp health, reflected in the types of products customers are seeking within the haircare category.’
Hair products with helpful amino acids - such as keratin and collagen - are flying off the shelves as customers are ‘increasingly ingredient-led’, Saunders added. This is similar to a trend for skincare, she said.
‘Concerns around thinning hair, shedding and density have pushed customers to seek out targeted solutions,’ she said. ‘As a result, demand for efficacy-led products is accelerating.’
Boots is also seeing more shoppers seeking products or routines they have discovered on social media.
Influencer and hair expert Abbey Yung - who is known for sharing an elaborate 11-step routine to her 3.1million followers - has caused certain products, such as a £21 ‘anti-hair loss scalp serum’ from Pantene, to do well.
Saunders added: ‘We’re seeing trichologists, dermatologists and pharmacists becoming the new influencers, and their impact is very real.’

items.title: M&S links up with Sephora to lure younger shoppers
items.summary: Beauty specialist will open branded areas in 100 Marks & Spencer stores and will sell its products on chain’s website Business live – latest updates Marks & Spencer is has signed a deal with Sephora to open areas under the beauty brand’s name within its stores, in its latest tactic to attract younger shoppers. The French retailer is set to launch branded areas staffed by Sephora employees in 100 M&S stores and sell through the British retailer’s website in spring next year. Continue reading...
items.body:
Marks & Spencer is has signed a deal with Sephora to open areas under the beauty brand’s name within its stores, in its latest tactic to attract younger shoppers.
The French retailer is set to launch branded areas staffed by Sephora employees in 100 M&S stores and sell through the British retailer’s website in spring next year.
Seophora relaunched in the UK in 2023 with huge fanfare and now has about 18 stand-alone British stores. The company is owned by LVMH, the luxury goods group led by Bernard Arnault, who with his family is among the world’s richest people with a $171bn (£129bn) fortune, according to Forbes.
The company has rapidly expanded on its second attempt to enter the UK market after closing a handful of stores in 2005, having failed make a dent in a competitive sector. The deal with M&S marks a new strategy in its expansion plans.
Analysts have said Sephora’s work with up-and-coming brands and collaborations with high-profile influencers on Instagram, TikTok, and YouTube has helped the brand reach its target female audience of 24- to 36-year-olds.
John Lyttle, the managing director of M&S’s fashion, home and beauty division, said: “Beauty is an important category for M&S, with the potential to attract new customers to shop with us and give existing customers the opportunity to shop with us more often.”
“Combining Sephora’s specialist expertise with the strength of the M&S brand, our store estate and our growing digital platform,” Lyttle said. “Alongside this, we will continue investing in our own-label beauty categories where we have established strength and customer trust.”
Retailers have been battling to grab a share of the beauty market after the disappearance of many department stores. In recent years a swathe of UK department stores have closed, including Debenhams, Beales and about half the House of Fraser chain.
Sephora’s self-service model – which allows consumers to touch and test makeup and perfume without the help of shop staff – is seen to appeal to younger shoppers, who may test in store and buy online. The tie-up could provide increased competition for the specialist health and beauty chains Boots and Superdrug.
Lyttle said the deal was part of M&S’s wider transformation plan, which involves £700m of investments in revitalising stores, modernising its supply chain and distribution system, and further improvements in products.
The group, which employs more than 65,000 people, has 227 full-line stores – containing food, clothing, homewares and beauty – after closing dozens of old and out-of-place outlets. More will shut over the next two years and a handful of new outlets are opening with the aim to have 200 full-line stores in the UK.
M&S’s food arm is expanding rapidly, with 18 food-only stores opening this year as it heads for a target of 420, compared with 335 directly operated outlets. Franchise partners run another 466 in the UK and more overseas.
Sarah Boyd, the managing director of Sephora UK, said: “Together, we can redefine what high street beauty means for customers across the UK, bringing the very best curated brand and beauty experience to the M&S stores.”
She said the group would introduce its beauty advisers to M&S stores to “provide a truly personalised experience, and to reach customers in more communities where they already live, shop and spend their time”.

items.body:
Jo Malone London announces the next chapter in its UK retail expansion, officially launching within Space NK.
From today, Tuesday 29th September 2026, the British fragrance and lifestyle house will be available in 26 Space NK stores nationwide and online at SpaceNK.com, bringing a curated edit of its most-loved scents to Space NK’s highly engaged beauty community.
Known for its joyfully British spirit, elegant craftsmanship and unexpected approach to fragrance, Jo Malone London brings its unrivalled olfactive offering to Space NK, encouraging discovery among consumers with a carefully considered edit that offers the perfect introduction to the world of Jo Malone London. The selection includes much-loved icons such as Lime Basil & Mandarin, English Pear & Freesia, Pomegranate Noir and Wood Sage & Sea Salt, alongside new favourites Sea Salt & Bergamot and Cypress & Grapevine Cologne Intense.
Speaking on the launch, Lizzie Brady, vice president general manager, Jo Malone London UK, says: “Launching with Space NK marks an exciting new chapter for Jo Malone London in the UK. Renowned for its carefully curated approach to beauty and highly engaged community, Space NK is a natural partner for us. This partnership gives us the opportunity to introduce Jo Malone London to new and existing consumers in a distinctive environment, through a considered edit of our most-loved scents, while staying true to the elevated experience and sense of discovery at the heart of our brand.”

The partnership is an important next step in the transformation of M&S Fashion, Home and Beauty, offering customers more of the beauty brands they love and a […] If you want more information Retail Times get in touch! items.body:
M&S today announces a strategic partnership with Sephora to create Sephora at M&S, a new beauty destination launching in selected M&S stores and on M&S.com from spring 2027.
The partnership is an important next step in the transformation of M&S Fashion, Home and Beauty, offering customers more of the beauty brands they love and a stronger specialist experience.
By bringing together Sephora’s beauty expertise, brand relationships and focus on discovery with M&S’s trusted brand, national presence and omnichannel platform, the partnership will make a specialist beauty experience accessible to more customers in more places. M&S will bring Sephora to 100 high streets and retail parks across the UK.
The new, transformed beauty offer will help attract new customers and give existing customers more reasons to shop with M&S more frequently.
For Sephora, the partnership marks the next step in its UK growth story, extending its prestige beauty experience into more communities through the UK’s most trusted brand*. Building on Sephora’s destination store, boutique and digital formats, the shop-in-shop retail model will give more customers access to curated brands, expert advice and the beauty discovery experience for which Sephora is known.
Customers can expect a carefully curated mix of established beauty favourites, emerging brands and exclusive products across skincare, makeup, fragrance, haircare and bodycare.
Specialist beauty teams will support customers in stores while M&S.com will offer a broader online range with home delivery and Click & Collect from M&S stores nationwide. The final brand line-up will be confirmed closer to launch, alongside details of new-to-M&S names and selected Sephora exclusives.
John Lyttle, managing director, Fashion, Home & Beauty at M&S, said: “We’re transforming Fashion, Home and Beauty at M&S, creating a better experience for our customers and building a more efficient, more profitable business. Our new partnership with Sephora is the next step in this transformation. Beauty is an important category for M&S, with the potential to attract new customers to shop with us and give existing customers the opportunity to shop with us more often.
“Our partnership with Sephora will sit at the heart of our future beauty offer, combining Sephora’s specialist expertise with the strength of the M&S brand, our store estate and our growing digital platform. Alongside this, we will continue investing in our own-label Beauty categories where we have established strength and customer trust.”
Catherine Spindler, president of Europe & Middle East, Sephora, said: “Sephora’s ambition has always been to continually evolve how we bring our expertise in beauty to market, adapting our global model to reflect the needs and opportunities of each region. In the UK, this has seen us build a deliberately complementary ecosystem across our digital and app proposition, large-format ‘Temples of Beauty’ and, most recently, our curated boutique concepts that debuted in London this summer.
“Our UK launch has been such a huge success, that we wanted to go further and faster. Our partnership with M&S is the next evolution of this strategy, introducing a retail model that complements our existing formats and allows us to build on the strength of the Sephora brand in the UK. By combining our global expertise in prestige beauty with M&S’s established retail infrastructure, we are creating a more diversified and scalable model for growth, while continuing to evolve the way customers can access the Sephora experience.”
Sarah Boyd, managing director, SEPHORA UK said: “Since bursting on to the scene in the UK, we have always believed that becoming part of the communities we serve means more than simply opening stores and having a great online experience. We have taken a deliberately local approach to every city we enter, from celebrating local culture and creators to tailoring our opening moments and marketing to reflect the people who live there. This personalisation has been a huge part of our success thus far, and now partnering with M&S, a brand so trusted, loved and deeply ingrained in British life is not just a great honour and privilege, but also an extremely exciting next step in our expansion journey.
“Together, we can re-define what high street beauty means for customers across the UK, bringing the very best curated brand and beauty experience to the M&S stores to complement their food, fashion and home expertise. We are excited to introduce our incredible Beauty Advisors to the stores to provide a truly personalised experience, and to reach customers in more communities where they already live, shop and spend their time.
“This partnership marks an important milestone in our continuing drive to become a truly winning formula on the UK High Street.”

items.title: Reform Senedd member visits Fed retailers in Tenby, West Wales
items.summary: Members of the Federation of Independent Retailers (The Fed), Vince and Fiona Malone, welcomed Senedd member Claire Archibald to their Tenby Store to show the vital role their shop and post office plays in their West Wales Community. After a career in healthcare, Archibald was… This story continues at Reform Senedd member visits Fed retailers in Tenby, West Wales Or just read more coverage at Talking Retail
items.body:
After a career in healthcare, Archibald was elected to the Senedd in May this year, elected to the Ceredigion Penfro constituency as a Reform candidate.
The meeting highlighted the social value of shops and post offices, with particular emphasis on the 650 post offices across Wales.
The Malones, of Morrisons Daily – Tenby Stores and Post Office, emphasised the particularly high cost of business – through a mix of high business rate costs and high commercial costs and energy bills – and how they make it increasingly difficult to sustain small retail businesses, despite their social value.
Mr and Mrs Malone also highlighted the launch of the Deposit Return Scheme for recycling bottles and cans when it goes live in October 2027 and the work the Fed is undertaking to help small shops prepare.
They also shared concerns about potential complexities in Wales linked to bringing glass into the scheme, which is scheduled to fully take effect after a longer four-year transition period until October 2031.
The Fed members also raised their concerns about retail crime and rogue trade on the High Street and reiterated the particular priority the Fed places on enhancing resources for Neighbourhood Policing and Local Authority trading standards.
Archibald said: “It was an extremely positive meeting and I look forward to working with Vince and Fiona in the future. I hope to meet with them again in the Senedd at some point and will also try and stop by the shop when I am in Tenby in the future!”
Vince and Fiona Malone added: “We would like to thank Claire for visiting us and for engaging openly on the issues affecting our business and community. The ball is now in the hands of the Senedd to ensure that these concerns are acted upon.”

items.title: Crew Clothing warns on consumer confidence as profit stalls
items.summary: Crew Clothing has warned that it could suffer from a significant slowdown in consumer confidence, as the retailer saw profit stall last year. The high street clothes seller said it is bracing for a potential drop-off in spending, as inflation fears caused by the Iran war tighten shoppers’ budgets.  In a statement the firm said: [...]
items.body:
Crew Clothing warns on consumer confidence as profit stalls
Crew Clothing has warned that it could suffer from a significant slowdown in consumer confidence, as the retailer saw profit stall last year.
The high street clothes seller said it is bracing for a potential drop-off in spending, as inflation fears caused by the Iran war tighten shoppers’ budgets.
In a statement the firm said: “The retail landscape remains a challenging trading space for many.
“Although Crew’s customers have shown great resilience in the past, the business remains cognisant of potential slowdown in consumer spending as a result of rises in the cost of living and economic pressures.”
The retailer’s pre-tax profit remained flat at £25.5m in 2025, despite turnover jumping by a fifth to £151m. The firm’s cost of sales rose by eight per cent to £44m.
Crew Clothing said its website outperformed its high street business last year, as online sales jumped by 30 per cent, compared to 21 per cent growth in its stores.
Retailers have warned that the summer’s record temperatures drove shoppers away from high streets, though online sellers benefited from the extreme heat.
‘Middle England’s Ralph Lauren’
Crew Clothing’s consumer confidence warning comes as the retail industry ramps up pressure on the government to boost high street businesses at next month’s Budget.
Andy Burnham has suggested he could cut business rates bills for smaller shops, but large retailers have warned that the Prime Minister must not hike taxes for big shops to fund this move.
Retailers have also urged the government to roll back recent hikes to employer national insurance contributions and the minimum wage, promising they will hire more young people if the cost of employment falls.
Crew Clothing was founded by Devon-based windsurfing instructor Alistair Parker-Swift in 1993.
In 2017, Parker-Swift and private equity firm Livingbridge sold their stakes in the retailer to US-based clothing manufacturer Exquisite Apparel.
The clothing group is controlled by Menoshi ‘Michael’ Shina, who led a group of investors in the £22.6m takeover of suitmaker Moss Bros in 2020.
Former Crew Clothing chief executive David Butler, who quit in 2023, had described the retailer as “middle England’s Ralph Lauren” as he set out plans to open new stores in market towns and coastal resorts.

items.title: Infobip predicts ~200 million Black Friday and Cyber Monday interactions in UK as AI reshapes the 2026 shopping season

Global AI-first cloud communications platform Infobip predicts that around 193 million messages will be sent from businesses to consumers across Black Friday and Cyber Monday 2026 in the UK. That’s as AI and conversational channels transform how consumers discover products, receive offers and access support. New global research also reveals that 63.2% of consumers have […] If you want more information Retail Times get in touch! Retail Times - Retail Times, a free to view retail news website
items.body:
Global AI-first cloud communications platform Infobip predicts that around 193 million messages will be sent from businesses to consumers across Black Friday and Cyber Monday 2026 in the UK. That’s as AI and conversational channels transform how consumers discover products, receive offers and access support.
New global research also reveals that 63.2% of consumers have used an AI assistant or chatbot while shopping during the past 12 months.
Black Friday is no longer a single shopping event. Infobip’s research shows that globally, the shopping season now begins weeks earlier and continues through the entire customer journey. Nearly six in ten respondents will have started holiday shopping by early November, while only 19% wait until Black Friday week itself. This extended shopping window is creating new pressure for retailers to engage customers earlier, with better timing, more relevant offers and frictionless support across the channels consumers already use.
AI is becoming a central part of that journey. According to the research, 63.2% of global consumers have used an AI assistant or chatbot for shopping in the last 12 months, with 21.9% using one frequently. Among consumers willing to use AI for shopping, 73.4% would use it to compare products and 67.8% would use it to find deals matching their preferences.
The data also suggests that while email remains a dominant channel for deals and updates in the UK, conversational and mobile channels are becoming increasingly important for time-sensitive, personalised retail engagement. Rich Communication Services (RCS) are predicted to see the biggest increase in volume in the UK, by over 280% this Black Friday.
James Stokes, Head of UK and Nordics at Infobip, said: “Black Friday is no longer a single day or even a single week. It has become an extended conversation between consumers and brands, beginning with discovery and continuing through purchase, delivery and support. AI gives retailers the opportunity to make those conversations faster, more relevant and more personal. The winners will be the brands that understand when, where and how each customer wants to engage.”

St. Ewe Free Range Eggs is continuing to drive premiumisation within the egg category with the national launch of its Rich Yolk Luxuriously Large 10-pack, which will roll out to 244 Tesco stores from 21st September.
The launch comes as consumer demand for premium eggs continues to grow, with shoppers increasingly willing to pay more for quality. According to the latest NielsenIQ data, 10-pack eggs are now the fastest-growing format in the category by value (+20%), followed by 12-packs (+12.3%), highlighting a clear shift towards larger premium packs as household demand for eggs continues to increase.
At the same time, consumers are buying eggs more frequently than ever before. Nielsen Homescan data shows the average shopper now purchases eggs 17.3 times per year, while spending per shopping occasion has increased by 7.5% year-on-year, demonstrating continued investment in the category despite wider economic pressures.
The new Rich Yolk Luxuriously Large 10-pack has been developed for consumers looking for a premium everyday egg, offering rich golden yolks, larger eggs and the quality synonymous with the St. Ewe brand.
Anthony Frankland, Head of Retail at St. Ewe Free Range Eggs comments: “This is an exciting new launch for everyone at St. Ewe. As shopper purchasing behaviour continues to evolve, it’s important that we do the same and ensure our range reflects what consumers are looking for. The data shows a growing demand for premium, high-quality egg products in larger volumes, and that’s exactly what this launch delivers. I can’t wait to see the standout packaging on shelves in-store and online.”
Bex Tonks, CEO and Farmer at St. Ewe Free Range Eggs, said: “We’re seeing a real shift in the way consumers shop the egg category. People are buying eggs more often, and they’re increasingly choosing to invest in higher-quality products that deliver on taste, versatility and eating experience. The launch of our Rich Yolk Luxuriously Large 10-pack into Tesco is another important milestone for the brand and reflects the continued premiumisation we’re seeing across the category. Consumers are recognising the value of great-quality eggs and looking for products that elevate everyday meals, whether that’s breakfast, baking or cooking from scratch.”
The Tesco launch builds on continued momentum for the St. Ewe Rich Yolk range, which has become increasingly popular with shoppers looking for richer flavour, vibrant golden yolks and premium quality.
The listing also reinforces St. Ewe’s strategy of driving innovation and premium growth within the category while responding to changing consumer shopping habits.

items.title: Usdaw welcomes home secretary’s ‘continuing commitment’ to tackling retail crime
items.summary: Retail trade union Usdaw welcomed the speech to Labour’s annual conference in Liverpool by Shabana Mahmood, home secretary, where she highlighted Labour’s achievements on retail crime and the government’s continuing commitment to neighbourhood policing. As part of her address to delegates, Mahmood's said: “Across the… This story continues at Usdaw welcomes home secretary’s ‘continuing commitment’ to tackling retail crime Or just read more coverage at Talking Retail
items.body:
As part of her address to delegates, Mahmood’s said: “Across the country, certain crimes, particularly those that tear at the fabric of a local community are still too high. Like shop theft, which though now falling, is still far too high.
“To achieve fairness in every community, we need to do some things we know work, like neighbourhood policing. Which was hollowed out under the Conservative government but which we know cuts crime and deters criminality.
“I am proud to say that this government has put 3,800 more officers into neighbourhoods across the country.”
Commenting after the speech, Joanne Thomas – Usdaw general secretary, said: “We very much welcome Labour’s investment in neighbourhood policing, to help tackle crime and anti-social behaviour in communities and town centres.
“Usdaw’s latest interim survey results show the level of attacks on retail workers remains high. It is shocking that nearly three-quarters of those working in retail are regularly facing abuse from customers, with far too many experiencing threats and violence.
“This is a hugely important issue for our members, and they are saying loud and clear that enough is enough.
“Labour’s investment in more uniformed officer patrols in shopping areas and neighbourhoods adds to the government’s extensive action to tackle retail crime. The Crime and Policing Act will deliver a much-needed protection of shop workers’ law; end the indefensible £200 threshold for prosecuting shoplifters, which has effectively become an open invitation to retail criminals; along with Criminal Behaviour Orders.
“There is also new funding to tackle the organised criminals responsible for the increase in shoplifting.
“We continue to call on the government to urgently bring these new measures into force, to give the police the tools to deal with the problem and help protect retail workers.”

items.title: New analysis uncovers stability of summer retail footfall across UK
items.summary: Discover what's happening in retail today, Retail Times publishes international & UK retail news covering products, data, tech, packaging, people, research, comment and much more. Summer may be over, but for retailers now digging into how the season performed, a new analysis of ONS weekly retail footfall data offers a useful benchmark. The study uncovers the stability of week-to-week shopper numbers across the UK’s regions over summer, finding Scotland to have some of the biggest variations in footfall for the […] If you want more information Retail Times get in touch! Retail Times - Retail Times, a free to view retail news website
items.body:
Summer may be over, but for retailers now digging into how the season performed, a new analysis of ONS weekly retail footfall data offers a useful benchmark. The study uncovers the stability of week-to-week shopper numbers across the UK’s regions over summer, finding Scotland to have some of the biggest variations in footfall for the second year in a row
The research, from point of sale provider Epos Now, used the ONS/BT Active Intelligence weekly footfall figures for June-August 2025 and 2026 to compare differences in annual performance. The study then measured two factors for each UK region (aside from Northern Ireland) to assess how footfall is performing; how much weekly footfall values varied relative to their average level over the period (stability), and how footfall this summer compared to the 2023 levels ONS index against (growth).
Scotland sees biggest variations in footfall, but growth is high
Scotland’s weekly footfall varied by 6.55% on average in summer 2026 and 6.22% in summer 2025. Footfall started summer 2026 slightly below its 2023 baseline before climbing to 20% above it by mid-August, which could have been driven by the likes of Edinburgh Fringe Festival, as one possibility. However, looking at how footfall is performing against 2023 averages that the ONS index against, on average Scottish retail saw weekly footfall increase by 5.49%. In comparison, in 2025 Scotland’s footfall grew by 2.84% on average each week over summer.
London’s footfall booms
Looking at footfall in London, the region’s weekly footfall was 17.5% above the 2023 average. The region also had fairly stable figures, with footfall varying by 3.44% away from its summer average, and was at its highest through 29th June – 19th July.
East of England’s footfall shows stability
The East of England demonstrated some of the most stable weekly footfall figures, with it varying weekly by 2.4% on its summer average. Alongside this, the region also saw growth of 4.71% on weekly footfall from 2023’s indexed average. However, this is down from the 7.3% weekly average footfall growth the region saw in 2025.
North East, North West, and Yorkshire show declines
Despite having low variations in weekly footfall, the North East, North West, and Yorkshire recorded declines in weekly footfall against their 2023 baseline through summer 2026. The North West saw average weekly footfall fall by 2.6% from 2023’s average, whilst the North East saw a 4% decline and Yorkshire a 5% decrease.
| Region | 2026 variation | 2026 Average weekly footfall vs 2023 baseline | 2025 variation | 2025 Average weekly footfall vs 2023 baseline | 
| UK total | 2.56% | 5.69% | 2.47% | 3.45% | 
| England | 2.54% | 6.02% | 2.56% | 3.48% | 
| East of England | 2.42% | 4.71% | 2.45% | 7.25% | 
| North East | 2.62% | -4.16% | 2.82% | 0.35% | 
| North West | 2.80% | -2.61% | 3.26% | 0.41% | 
| Yorkshire and The Humber | 2.81% | -5.37% | 3.69% | -0.49% | 
| East Midlands | 2.88% | 1.54% | 3.39% | 4.17% | 
| West Midlands | 3.10% | 1.40% | 3.28% | 4.06% | 
| South East | 3.33% | 2.56% | 2.30% | 2.54% | 
| London | 3.44% | 17.53% | 4.13% | 5.13% | 
| Wales | 4.22% | 1.03% | 3.34% | 5.04% | 
| South West | 4.49% | 1.06% | 3.35% | 3.32% | 
| Scotland | 6.55% | 5.49% | 6.22% | 2.84% | 
Jacyn Heavens, CEO at Epos Now, comments, “Footfall across retail has seen fluctuations through the summer months caused by extreme heat and seasonal sporting events, however, the number of regions showing growth on the 2023 averages that the ONS benchmark against shows promising hope for highstreets, retail parks and the like. As we move into the golden quarter of the year for retail, it’s important that retailers focus on understanding and using their real time sales data to forecast for the likes of footfall, stock, and staffing.”
